case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free.
